The same number as an EAN-13 barcode (prefix 978):

Look for the math

The last digit of a book number is not chosen freely — it is a checksum that catches mistakes.

The mod-11 check

A ten-digit ISBN satisfies 10d₁ + 9d₂ + … + 2d₉ + d₁₀ ≡ 0 (mod 11). Given the first nine digits, the last is forced. If it comes out to 10, it is written X. The logic test checks the formula on real ISBNs such as 0-306-40615-2 and 0-8044-2957-X, and confirms that changing one digit breaks the check. The page's formatting rules are also enforced: three hyphens, none consecutive, and one just before the check digit.

Two independent checks

An ISBN-10 appears in a barcode by prepending 978 to its nine digits and appending a new check digit, computed with weights 3 and 1 to make the total a multiple of 10. The two check digits are unrelated: the embedding only reuses the first nine digits. The test confirms the new check digit and that the 95 black-and-white modules decode back to the EAN-13.

Cycle one digit and watch the last cell change. Why does a single wrong digit always get caught?
